Why RSS Never Actually Died, It Just Went Quiet

By Priya Nathan · Staff Writer · Published March 4, 2026

When Google shut down Reader in 2013, obituaries for RSS were written across the tech press with something close to relish. The feed icon, once a fixture in every browser toolbar, was declared a relic of the early web: a format built for a slower, less social internet that had simply been outgrown. A decade on, the epitaphs look premature. RSS did not die. It went underground, and then it quietly became the plumbing for half the software you use today.

Start with podcasts. Every episode you download, whether through Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Overcast, or a dozen smaller apps, is delivered by an RSS feed generated the moment a show is published. There is no alternative protocol competing for that job; RSS simply won it by default and never had to defend the title, because nobody in the podcast industry ever proposed replacing it. The format's obituary writers were, in a narrow but important sense, describing the death of a user interface, not the death of the underlying plumbing.

Newsletters tell a similar story from the other direction. Substack, Beehiiv, and ConvertKit built businesses on top of email, but nearly every one of them quietly exposes an RSS feed alongside the inbox delivery, because power users demanded it and because feed readers remain the fastest way to triage a large volume of writing without a subject line fighting for your attention in a crowded inbox. The format never needed a marketing department; it needed people who read enough to feel the pain that a good feed reader solves.

What actually changed after 2013 was not the technology but the audience. Reader's death coincided with the rise of algorithmic social feeds, and for most casual readers, an engagement-optimized timeline was simply more fun to scroll than a chronological list of unread items. RSS lost the mainstream not because it was technically inferior, but because it asked something the mainstream had stopped wanting to give: a deliberate, curated list of sources you chose yourself, rather than one a ranking algorithm chose for you.

That tradeoff is exactly what is bringing a smaller, more deliberate audience back. As social feeds have become noisier and increasingly hostile to outbound links, a growing number of people who read for a living, or who simply got tired of doom-scrolling, are rebuilding the reading habits Reader once supported. The difference this time is the addition of a layer Reader never had: cheap language models that can summarize, deduplicate, and rank a personal feed without shipping your reading history to an advertiser. Self hosted readers paired with a small AI pipeline can now do quietly, for a few dollars a month, what used to require a team at Google.

None of this means RSS is about to reclaim the mainstream; the format is never going to out-compete a short-video feed for casual attention, and it was never trying to. But for the smaller audience that reads with intent, the underlying infrastructure that carried a decade of podcasts and newsletters without anyone noticing is now getting a reader worth using again. The feed icon may never return to the browser toolbar, but the feeds themselves never actually left.
